analysis.one_liner: Charges a per-ton fee on coal, oil, and natural gas and returns the money as payroll tax cuts.
analysis.headline: The carbon tax bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tax coal, petroleum, and natural gas at $10 per ton of carbon dioxide starting in 2016, rising $10 each year. The money would first help workers in industries hurt by the tax, then fill shortfalls in the Highway Trust Fund, with the rest returned to individuals as a rebate of the payroll taxes they paid. It also placed fees on imports of carbon-intensive goods so foreign competitors would not have an advantage, and called for binding international agreements to cut greenhouse gases.
analysis.who_benefits: Working taxpayers get a refundable credit equal to their share of the carbon tax revenue, capped at the payroll taxes they paid or 10% of their Social Security benefits, which would cut taxes on work. Workers in coal, oil, and gas industries would receive transition assistance during the first decade. Highway and transit funding would get new revenue to cover shortfalls. Everyone benefits from reduced carbon pollution.

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives individual taxpayers a refundable credit, the 'carbon tax rebate,' equal to their per-capita share of the carbon tax revenue, capped at the greater of the payroll taxes they paid or 10% of their Social Security benefits [S3].
The first slice of carbon tax revenue is reserved for transition assistance to workers in industries negatively affected by the tax, phased down over a decade and ending after 2025 [S3].
The next slice covers Highway Trust Fund shortfalls, addressing a chronic funding gap for roads and transit [S3].
The tax starts at $10 per metric ton of carbon dioxide in 2016 and rises $10 per year, creating a steadily increasing incentive to shift away from coal, oil, and natural gas [S3].
Border adjustments place an equivalent fee on imported carbon-intensive goods like steel, cement, aluminum, and paper, and rebate the cost to exporters, so U.S. manufacturers are not undercut [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers, producers, and importers of coal, petroleum, and natural gas pay the new excise tax, and the cost passes to consumers through higher prices for electricity, gasoline, heating fuel, and carbon-intensive goods. Households whose energy costs rise more than their payroll-tax rebate, such as heavy fuel users, would lose out.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The tax raises the price of gasoline, electricity, and heating fuel, and because energy is a larger share of spending for lower-income households, the burden falls hardest on those who use the most fuel [S3].

The rebate is capped at the payroll taxes an individual paid or 10% of Social Security benefits, so households with large energy bills but limited payroll-tax liability could end up paying more in energy costs than they get back [S3].
Transition assistance for workers in affected industries shrinks each year and reaches zero after 2025, leaving coal communities without support even as the tax keeps rising $10 annually [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design returns most of the revenue to working people through payroll-tax relief and protects export industries with border adjustments, which is a serious attempt to make a carbon tax progressive rather than simply a price hike. But the rising tax would still raise living costs for fuel-heavy households the rebate formula does not fully cover, and long-term support for coal and oil communities phases out. Whether the gains outweigh the costs depends on how fast families can cut their fuel use.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means and Foreign Affairs Committees, where it sat with zero cosponsors and no hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson introduced the bill on July 31, 2014, and it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Foreign Affairs Committee [S1][S5].
Neither committee took any further action on the bill before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and gas producers and importers avoided a new carbon tax, and energy consumers avoided the price increases it would have brought. Working taxpayers did not get the payroll-tax cut, and the Highway Trust Fund shortfall remained unaddressed by this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers dodged the tax

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its carbon tax, trust fund, and payroll-tax rebate framework.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill.

against.name: House Foreign Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for the international provisions and took no action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape of the opposition never showed up in the record.

industries.note: Coal would be taxed at the full carbon rate starting in 2016, and coal has the highest carbon content per unit of energy, so the tax burden on coal would be the heaviest and would grow every year. Blocking the bill preserved coal's price position against cleaner energy sources.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: Petroleum, petroleum products, and natural gas would be taxed per ton of carbon content at the point of sale, manufacture, or import, raising the cost of gasoline and heating fuels. The industry's interest in stopping the bill ran against the rebate and pollution benefits the public would have received.

The bill would transfer carbon tax revenue to cover Highway Trust Fund shortfalls, split between the Highway Account and Mass Transit Account, funding road and transit projects. Stopping the bill left that funding gap unaddressed.

These industries would pay more for energy but the bill includes border adjustment fees on competing imports and rebates for exports to keep them competitive, so their net exposure was limited. They still bore higher domestic energy costs.
